answers.name: Linda Buchanan
answers.answer:
Thank you for your email and for the reminder.
I would look to explore and implement the following:
* I will mention education because this is the first step we take in the City when addressing matters but will look to go beyond reactive messaging.
* I believe we need to be very proactive in our education including materials provided with business licences; retail stores that have outdoor food stalls, restaurants, garden stores and with outside waste haulers etc.
* Wildlife Awareness Information can be provided with annual garbage schedules as reminders to people https://www.cnv.org/home-property/garbage-recycling-green-can/wildlife-awareness - including stickers that can be placed on garbage cans/organic waste bins as weekly reminders; cleaning and sanitizing;freezing etc. plus stickers from staff when garbage/organic bins are not put out properly. Strengthen compliance.
* In the City, under local nuisance and waste bylaws, businesses are completely responsible for managing their wildlife attractants. Outdoor dumpsters and bins (including oil) must remain tightly closed, locked, or housed within heavy-duty, gated commercial enclosures. Strengthen attractant management. During spring, summer and fall regular check-ins with businesses should become standard practice. Fines should proceed for non-compliance and a plan established to mitigate for the future.
* Support Partnerships. Connect BIA's with North Shore Bear Advocates and North Shore Black Bear Society to work with retail outlets, restaurants to support them with managing wildlife attractants through walk-throughs
* Explore with NS Bear Advocates and NS Black Bear Society what would be an appropriate response protocol when there is a bear in the urban setting. How can we track sightings, and safely relocate in a preventative way as opposed to having to react. City assessment and plan.
* I would like to explore what other urban cities are doing to reduce the conflict and co-exist.
Thank you for the opportunity to respond.

answers.name: Oliver King
answers.answer:
Bears act on instinct. Humans have the ability to think, plan and adapt. I do not believe bears should be killed for simply behaving according to their natural instincts.
We are the ones who must learn how to live alongside wildlife. That means better planning, prevention, securing attractants and finding ways to keep people and bears safely separated when necessary.
Bears have a right to exist too. I am a strong defender of wildlife, and I am against killing bears. Our responsibility should be to find humane ways to coexist with them, not destroy them.

answers.name: Dave Kurvers
answers.answer:
Thank you for writing. I agree that education alone isn’t enough.
I lived in an area with regular bear activity. I’ve had fences knocked down and watched bears return year after year to investigate the same spots.
I would pursue weekly garbage collection in areas where bears habitate, like ravines and creeks, particularly during months when bears are active, alongside weekly Green Can collection. I’d ask staff to cost a seasonal program, measure whether it reduces bear-related garbage incidents, and examine better secure-storage options where problems recur.
Residents have a responsibility to manage attractants, but the City also needs to design its waste collection system around the community we actually live in.
I would rather invest in preventing bears from becoming food-conditioned than continue seeing bears destroyed after the problem develops. I also beleive that this issue is greater in the district vs the City.

answers.name: Mike McGraw
answers.answer:
Thanks for asking this, and for the reminder. Three bears killed in one week tells us education alone isn't working, and in almost every case the cause is something people can control.
The City already has some of the right rules. Our solid waste bylaw says carts can't go out before 5:30 a.m. on collection day and that containers must keep animals out, with fines up to $2,000. But those rules don't mention wildlife, and they don't cover fruit trees, bird feeders or other attractants. Here's what I'd push for:
A wildlife attractant bylaw that covers garbage, green bins, fallen fruit, bird feeders and unsecured dumpsters, with bylaw officers actively enforcing the set-out rules we already have, starting in neighbourhoods near ravines and greenbelts where bears come into the City.
Bear-resistant containers as the standard for City public bins along greenbelts and trails, and for multi-family and commercial buildings, with a reasonable phase-in. As a strata president, I believe most buildings will do it if the rule is clear.
A partnership with volunteer gleaning groups so residents can get help picking fruit they can't use before it drops.
One North Shore approach. Bears move between all three municipalities, and the District has already done the work to be recognized as a Bear Smart Community. The City should align its rules with the District and West Vancouver, share sighting and conflict data with the Conservation Officer Service and WildSafeBC, and report publicly on whether conflicts are going down.

answers.name: Holly Back
answers.answer:
Hello, LT & Lindsey
Thank you for the opportunity to respond to your question regarding bear coexistence.
Bears are part of life on the North Shore, and I strongly believe we need to do everything possible to prevent bears from being euthanized because of human-bear conflicts. I would support bear-resistant garbage and organics containers, better education about attractants, early intervention, and working closely with conservation officers and wildlife organizations. We need to take responsibility for reducing attractants and give bears wthe best chance to remain wild and safe.

answers.name: Don Bell
answers.answer:
Thanks for your email re co-existing with bears.
I believe education is extremely important because many of the people who have spoken to me think they are being supportive of bears, coyotes and racoons by actually hand feeding them or at least putting “food” out for these wild animals.
It is important for the public to learn they are not “helping” bears. Instead, they are actually teaching the bears that deliberate feeding, or leaving food garbage available, is an easier food source than scrounging in the forest. Encouraging bears to urban settings can turn out deadly for the bears, small pets, children and adults.
But, as you point out, there needs to be more than just education.
I will ask Council and City staff to review what kind of bear-proof” lockable containers we can require be used, ideally located behind closed doors.
I will ask that Council consider increasing the bylaw penalties for either deliberately feeding bears or leaving compost garbage easily accessible by bears.
Until recently, we have not had many frequent visitation from bears, but it seems this year there has been more interactions.
I will request we contact other municipalities who have more bear visitations to see what we can apply in our city.
I would be interested if you have any specific recommendations that we could consider.

answers.name: Tammy Bentz
answers.answer:
I LOVE your work and I’m so appreciative that you are out there, keeping your eye on our bears.
I would fully support ways to keep our bears alive and transported back to homes rather than being shot (like the one in lower Lonsdale, mere days ago)!
I have not had much time to research this growing issue and I will definitely get back to you on what concrete measures I’d support taking, but in the meantime, may I ask you the question back? You would be the very person that I would like to seek guidance from since you know this topic more than I do!! As a city, what do we need to do to help keep our bears in the safety of the forests and away from our garbage/streets? Please advise.
If I were on Council now, I’d meet with you and invite you to present some options at the next Council Meeting. I’d find out the important info from you and then work to make that happen.
Do you have time for a phone call today or tomorrow? Please feel free to try me at the number below.
Thanks again for all your work and dedication. I look forward to more discussion with you to devise a plan with a concrete action plan,

answers.name: Anna Boltenko
answers.answer:
Thank you for asking this important question. I was heartbroken by the killing of the bear seen throughout Lower Lonsdale today. Bears are not intruders in our community—we share this place with them. We have a responsibility to prevent human-created attractants from turning their presence in our neighbourhoods into a death sentence.
Beyond education, my concrete commitment would be to strengthen the City’s waste system through a comprehensive Bear-Smart and Wildlife Attractant Action Plan. I would ask Council to:
* Phase in certified bear-resistant garbage and organics containers, beginning near ravines, creeks and known wildlife corridors, while upgrading public bins and requiring secure dumpsters for multi-family and commercial properties.
* Provide rebates or a container-loan program so seniors, lower-income households, renters, stratas and non-profits can comply without carrying an unfair cost.
* Strengthen proactive bylaw enforcement while helping people comply: practical assistance and warnings first, followed by meaningful penalties for repeated violations. The City should also provide clear, multilingual guidance for residents, stratas, property managers and businesses on securing waste, responding safely to bear sightings and protecting both people and wildlife.
* Complete a Bear Hazard Assessment and establish a coordinated response protocol with the other North Shore municipalities, the Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Nation, the North Shore Black Bear Society and the Conservation Officer Service. This should include rapid neighbourhood alerts, attractant inspections, shared data and non-lethal intervention wherever public safety permits.
The City already has morning collection rules and secure-storage requirements. The missing piece is ensuring that every household and business has the proper equipment, information and support—and that repeated non-compliance has consequences.
Nearby communities, including Squamish, Lions Bay, Port Moody, Coquitlam and Whistler, have demonstrated that education must be backed by bear-resistant waste infrastructure, enforceable attractant bylaws, neighbourhood monitoring and a coordinated response. North Vancouver should learn from these models and adapt the strongest measures to our more urban setting.
The municipality cannot control every decision made by provincial wildlife authorities. But it can act much earlier, before a bear becomes food-conditioned and the available options narrow dramatically. We should measure success by fewer dangerous encounters, safer residents and fewer bears killed.
I believe we can—and must—do better.

answers.name: David Brun
answers.answer:
Apologies for the late reply.
As a long-time resident and supporter of keeping our communities free of bear attractants, it is always heartbreaking for everyone involved when the outcome is for a bear to be euthanized.
Properly managing and storing garbage and compost so that bears cannot access them is vital to preventing these situations. Living with nature truly at our doorstep is both a privilege and a responsibility, and it is one that we all need to understand and take seriously.
I hope that, as a community, we can continue to do our part to reduce human-bear conflicts and help protect the bears that share our community.

answers.name: Angela Girard
answers.answer:
Thank you for the opportunity to provide respond to your question as a councillor candidate for the City of North Vancouver.
In response to your question, most of the North Shore's bear conflict is in the Districts of North Vancouver and West Vancouver, but bears do come down our ravines into the City. When they find garbage behind a townhouse complex, regrettably it is usually the bear that pays for it. Here are three actions I would suggest the City take:
1) Give City bylaws real force - the City already requires garbage and green cans to be stored where wildlife can't reach them. I would add a morning-only set-out window similar to the District, and match District fines. The bylaw should be consistent across municipal boundaries when a bear crosses it.
2) From my career in strata management, shared bins at townhouses and multi-family buildings are where this problem concentrates. As we add homes, wildlife-secure waste rooms should be a condition of approval. Existing strata/rental buildings next to ravines should possibly receive City support to retrofit.
3) There should be focus on ravine edge - fruit gleaning on City land, fencing standards for backyard hens and hives, and bear-resistant bins in parks along the ravine greenways.
A fourth, long-term goal, would be for the City to pursue Bear Smart status, as the District has, and publish the results every year.
Thank you again for the opportunity to respond to this important issue.

answers.name: Guy Heywood
answers.answer:
Besides education, we need a unified North Vancouver approach to preventing bear encounters and then we need to react better and faster when they happen. The bears come with the nature that surrounds North Vancouver and is like the biggest reason that it got it the most livable City* ranking. (*the survey ignored the City/District distinction...we should too!)
Parks and Environment planning, operations and staffing should be one professional organization accountable to the two local governments at a board level.. like the Museum & Archives or Rec Commission (used to be).
I am running in the City but my heart is in all North Vancouver.
All the best,

Lindsyvr@gmail.com...checking to see that I got the email address correct.
I've been hiking in the backcountry for 50 years. There have been encounters with black bears, sometimes, like in the middle of the night sniffing around the tent, they have been a little nerve-wracking, but food was always in a cache or high up in a tree and there has not been a problem.
Grizzlies scare me a little but they are not a issue here.
If we, as the best place to live in Canada, want to get properly prepared to welcome tourists and introduce them to the nature around us, we have to clean up our own act first.
Tourism North Shore does not work inside boundaries created for selfish reasons over a 100 years ago, The RCMP is all North Vancouver. For goodness sake North Shore Search and Rescue is not going to ask you which municipality you live in before they pull you out of the bush! As an old idiot that spent 9 years on the School Board, 7 years on the Recreation Commission, 6 years very frustrating years on the Council of a small-minded, selfish City government...I wish the rest of my community could see the opportunity there is for North Vancouver to bootstrap itself out of a truly horrible financial situation by coming together as a community (fixing our governments along the way).

answers.name: Ken Izatt
answers.answer:
Thanks for reaching out and asking me about the bear population.
As you know feeding bears is a problem and is illegal to do so. Garbage bears is also a problem. Not so much for people but with a habitual garbage fed bear usually does not end well for the bear.
I would like to see the conservation services more active in relocating problem bears rather than euthenize them. Although provinvially funded , we as a city can ask the conservation services for nore accountability.
We need to ensure that garbage is put out for pickup only in the morning of the collection day and use containers that are sealed.
We also have problems with fruit trees. To often residents allow mature fruit to drop to the ground and they leave it there. We need a bylaw that we can enforce fruit pick up and disposal if necessary. There are people that work for food distribution organizations that will come amd pick fruit to distribute to these in need. We can promote this service to residents.
We can enact a by-laws and ensure compliace with garbage disposal and fruit trees.

answers.name: Jullian Kolstee
answers.answer:
Thanks for reaching out and engaging with the municipal election on this important issue. I've never had a bear encounter in the city personally, nor have I been a homeowner with a property for bears to venture into, so I haven't had direct contact with bear advocacy before. I've looked into this and it seems there are already some potential mechanisms beyond education available:
- The Bear Smart Community Program offers clear steps that the city could follow to achieve Bear Smart status
- Bylaws exist but appear to lack sufficint enforcement, this is something the next council could address with harsher penalties and by eliminating warnings and issuing more fines
- I have personally seen unpicked fruit on properties that are not handled responsibly, so I would ask staff to find out what the scale of that problem is and how we might address it through the city
- Reviewing standards for waste bins that are not secured from bears, perhaps this had not been considered a high risk in the past, but the need seems to be increasing
- You mentioned that you weren't interested in education based solutions, but I'm interested in increasing civic literacy broadly, and I believe wildlife awareness should be part of that, we certainly have advocacy groups on the North Shore we could partner with on that
I hope I've been able to answer your question, but I have a lot to learn about how the city manages protecting bears, and it seems like the city has catching up to do. I think like most residents I have a fondness for bears and how they represent the uniqueness of our community, I'm certainly in favour of whatever we can do to protect them and the safety of the public.

answers.name: Max Lai
answers.answer:
If it were up to me, I think we don't need to look to far in how we can have better mechanisms and policies to better co-exist with bears such as looking at the BC Bear Smart Community Program and its resources as well as taking inspiration from Lions Bay, a community that is known to be certified with well-designed bear smart programs.
I think we should easily follow and adapt how Lions Bay has done it (as they are a community that has the same issues with us for bears), and use their strategy such as implementing a Bear Smart Committee via the North Vancouver Community Safety Advisory Committee to create a Human/Bear Conflict Management Plan with policies that range from more enforcement on garbage and recycling bylaws so bears don't get easier access to our garbage, whether it be residential or businesses, to policies that look to have consistent, long-term bear tracking to ensure that we know where our bears move naturally and to ensure their movement is not inhibited by our need to densify so their natural behavior isn't altered to depend on our food waste.
Hope this helps!  Max Lai

answers.name: Jessica McIlroy
answers.answer:
It has definitely been a busy bear year! The bear hanging around my street in Central Lonsdale has been getting a lot of attention.
In the City the rules around garbage and food attractants haven't been as strict as the District since we historically haven't had the same level of activity. But it's time to revisit that.
The North Shore Black Bear Society has good information on what can be done to better co-exist with bears:
https://northshorebears.com/living-with-bears/
I think the first thing to do is address garbage bins, starting with City bins in parks and public spaces. We could do the same as Whistler does and still have public garbage disposal places but make sure they are bear safe. Then we need to start looking at residential garbage and recycling bins and update the guidance on where they are kept and when they are brought out for pick up.
The Society does a wonderful job educating the public at community events but we could support them more to ensure residents are aware of their role in co-existing with bears and keeping them safe.

answers.name: Krishna Raisinghani
answers.answer:
Thanks for reaching out. I’ve been really saddened by the recent incidents involving people and bears across the North Shore. It’s heartbreaking to see these conflicts often end with another bear being killed.
This is personal for me too, since we recently had a bear break through our fence trying to get to a neighbour’s garbage bin. We mentioned it to them and they did not take any further action.
Beyond education, I would push for a stronger wildlife-attractant bylaw and a Bear Conflict Hotspot Response. When a bear is repeatedly accessing garbage in an area, the City should quickly send bylaw staff into that neighbourhood, identify unsecured garbage, organics, fallen fruit and other attractants, require them to be secured, and use escalating enforcement for repeat violations.
I’d also like to see bear-resistant garbage and organics storage become the standard, starting in areas with repeated conflicts, and require proper bear-resistant waste enclosures in new multi-family or commercial developments. Many neighbouring municipalities outside the City of North Vancouver currently use these.
While wildlife response itself is provincial, I would advocate for safe non-lethal options, including tranquilization where wildlife professionals determine it’s appropriate.
We share this community with bears, so I think our responsibility is to remove the conditions that draw them into conflict before another bear pays the price.

answers.name: Andrew Robertson
answers.answer:
Thank you for your email. Like many North Vancouverites, I share your concerns and agree this is an important issue for North Vancouver to address. I only just read there was a bear shot this morning in Lower Lonsdale, of all places, which is tragic.
Properly addressing challenges like this requires assessing the root causes and then applying targeted solutions. In my opinion, the best solutions come from subject matter experts — wildlife professionals and advocacy groups in this case. I’m not an expert in this area so I won’t pretend that I know what the best solution is.
I see the Council’s role as ensuring the right people are given the right resources to address our challenges using the right values. If there are solutions besides increased education and enforcement/bylaws for removing bear attractants (food waste, tree fruit) from private property, or more resources for ensuring attractants are removed from City property, then I would be very keen to hear them and explore how the City of North Vancouver could implement them.

answers.name: Shervin Shahriari
answers.answer:
I am saddened by the news of bears being killed after coming into our urban areas. I believe we should do everything possible to avoid that outcome. A concrete step I would take is to put forward a Council motion asking staff to look at practices in other municipalities with bear activity, identify successful approaches, and explore opportunities to work with the District of North Vancouver and possibly the District of West Vancouver, since bears move across municipal boundaries. New proactive measures could also be informed by bear activity and attractant data from the North Shore Black Bear Society, helping us identify emerging hotspots in the City and focus our efforts where they are most needed. In addition to better education this could include enforcement, higher penalties for deliberate feeding or accessible attractants, and improved garbage and compost storage.
When a bear does enter an urban area, I would like us to explore alternatives to killing it. As part of the motion, I would ask staff to examine whether a coordinated North Shore approach could provide access to a Conservation Officer to tranquilize and humanely relocate a bear when appropriate, and report on the feasibility, costs and risks.
I am happy to learn more about this issue and about recent practices that may have worked elsewhere. The goal is to reduce attractants and, when bears do enter our neighbourhoods, do everything reasonably possible to avoid a lethal outcome.

answers.name: Tony Valente
answers.answer:
Thank you for your patience Lindsey.
I agree that living on the North Shore means accepting that we live in bear country, and our goal should be to reduce the human behaviours and attractants that put bears at risk. I was saddened to hear of the destruction of the bear in the City this week.
Beyond education, I would support stronger attractant management and enforcement. That includes ensuring garbage and organics are securely stored, addressing repeat problem properties, and using our bylaws where education and voluntary compliance have not worked. Garbage, organics, bird feeders and fruit trees are among the attractants that can encourage bears to remain in residential areas.
I would also support reviewing whether additional bear-resistant waste infrastructure is needed in our parks. We should have staff work closely with the North Shore Black Bear Society to identify hotspots and target municipal action. The Society already collects reports on bear activity and attractants across the North Shore, which can help direct resources where they are most needed.
For us to live together we need to reduce the opportunities for bears to obtain human food before their behaviour changes and the consequences become irreversible. I believe municipalities have an important role to play in supporting residents and sometimes enforcing the rules when necessary.

answers.name: Stephan Nieweler
answers.answer:
The death of bears because of interactions with human activities is a significant problem in the District of North Vancouver. Current policies and protocols must be revisited based on best practice in other jurisdictions with similar issues.
Education is an important tool for reducing human-bear conflict, as new and some existing residents may not have dealt with wildlife issues in other cities or other parts of Metro Vancouver, prior to their move to North Vancouver. The forms of education utilized should be reviewed, however, in order to maximize their effectiveness and target a broader cross-section of District residents.
Aside from education, we must focus on household, commercial and municipal waste infrastructure, as well as regulations pertaining to the time waste is located at the curbside. It would be beneficial for the municipality to facilitate the supply of bear resistant bins, potentially reducing the cost for users through bulk purchase. The time that these bins are located at the roadside on collection day should also be reviewed, in order to minimize the opportunity for bears to interact with waste. The applicability and level of fines should be reviewed in order to increase compliance.
We should also take planning and maintenance measures to reduce the opportunity for bears to enter human occupied areas, including the strategic use of bear resistant fencing at the urban-nature interface, buffer zones where berries bush growth is minimized, the elimination of urban sprawl and the acquisition of strategic properties to enhance the connectivity of natural areas.

answers.name: Daniel Anderson
answers.answer: We need better waste storage protocols and enforcement: bears are drawn by the promise of food and the best thing we can do is remove that incentive.

answers.name: Trey Bell
answers.answer:
Thank you for reaching out. I am Dismayed by the number of bears being killed in our community. Beyond education, one of my biggest priorities is protecting the habitat that bears and other wildlife depend on. I am one of the few candidates in the DNV municipal election, who has been consistently speaking up for stronger protection of our forests and against continued urban sprawl. I believe this is directly connected to keeping bears safer on the North Shore. When forests and large stands of mature trees are removed for development, we continue reducing and fragmenting wildlife habitat and increasing interactions between bears and people.
If elected, I would advocate for stronger protection of our remaining forests and natural areas and oppose further urban sprawl into these areas. I also believe we need to listen to the organizations that have spent years working on bear coexistence. I have met with the North Shore Black Bear Society (NSBBS) as a candidate, and I also have a personal connection to the organization, as my father Kevin Bell was formerly co-chair of the NSBBS Board of Directors.
From my meeting with the North Shore Black Bear Society, I learned that the District needs to take more concrete action around waste management in townhouse strata communities, where human-bear conflicts have been increasing. This is an area where the DNV can be more proactive by working with strata communities to improve waste storage and management practices before conflicts occur and utilize existing bylaws if strata’s aren’t taking appropriate actions.
I would engage directly with the North Shore Black Bear Society on the specific municipal measures they believe would be most effective, and work to implement practical recommendations within the District’s jurisdiction. I would also advocate for the creation of a North Shore-wide committee that brings together representatives from all three municipal councils, organizations such as the North Shore Black Bear Society, and the Provincial Government. Bears do not recognize municipal boundaries, so protecting them requires a coordinated approach that gets everyone working together toward consistent policies and practical solutions across the North Shore. My priorities would be keeping forests standing, protecting wildlife habitat, reducing preventable human-bear conflicts, and doing everything we reasonably can to keep both bears and people safe. Thanks again for your question and I hope we can elect municipal leaders that take this issue seriously across the North Shore.

answers.name: Mathew Bond
answers.answer:
The deaths of so many bears this year is absolutely tragic. We live alongside a beautiful wilderness and have a responsibility to coexist with all of its natural inhabitants, including bears. I know the District already has very stringent wildlife attractant bylaws and actively enforces them, as I was on Council when these bylaws were updated. And this year we are seeing more an unusually high number of bears venture deeper into urban areas where they would not typically be seen if the natural foods they rely on were plentiful.
To be honest, I'm not a bear behavior expert, and I don't have a specific solution. If there isn't any food for the bears in the forest how do we prevent conflicts in urban areas? If they have no other choice, bears will eventually find food in an urban area no matter how locked down our bylaws on garbage, organic waste and attractants are or how hard we enforce them. I expect this will continue to be an issue as our climate warms and the natural landscape that used to provide food sources for bears changes, and I think its important to work on a solution. So I would support hearing from any experts that understand bear behavior in a warming climate, and coming up with a practical community response that allows us to coexist with bears, keeps people safe and keeps bears alive and in their natural habitat.

answers.name: Daina Boyd
answers.answer: Hi Lindsay thanks for the email. I am so saddened by the recent deaths of bears around the north shore. I live off Seymour River and we see bears often. I think education is key and we need actual bear proof garbage cans to avoid having them become to habituated.

answers.name: Betty Forbes
answers.answer:
I am running for my third term as Councillor for the District of North Vancouver.
It was heartwarming to read your letter about co-existing with North Shore Bears. Education is very important but to protect the bears/cubs more has to be done. You are absolutely correct about the many causes of the increased larger numbers of bears breaching our urban containment boundary, but it comes down to food, especially before hibernation. There have been so many mother bears killed leaving their cubs to die from starvation, killed by other bears, & wildlife as they are too young to have learnt all their life lessons from mom. Cubs usually stay with their mom until 18 months old. The COS either kills them, leaves them wherever they are found, and even when a wildlife sanctuary with room to take the cubs offers to take them, the COS often withholds permission to let them go to the help offered. The cubs perish.
Two years ago I submitted a motion to my council requesting changes (5) that I wanted to get passed for more humane treatment of these sentient beings. It passed. The resolution was then presented to the Lower Mainland Local Government Association (LMLGA) and was passed. This meant that the motion would go forward as a resolution to the Union of BC Municipalities (UBCM) annual convention. At this convention I attended a presentation by Conservation Officer Services (COS)(this is the Provincial body who makes the decision on how bears are treated, abandoned, killed. I then went to where all the municipality members go to hear the resolutions being presented and the sponsering municipality speaks in favor of their resolution (me on behalf of District of North Vancouver) and then the floor is open to everyone who wishes to speak (For / Against). Then the vote was called ... and it didn't pass.
Had it passed, UBCM would have adopted it and sent it to the Provincial Ministry who oversees the COS for review, implementation. I had worked on this for a year and was heartbroken.
I have connected with many people who are experts about bears. I have also connected with Councillors in other municipalities. Recently I connected with a Councillor and we have both agreed to work towards a Sea-to-Sky (North Van to Whistler) safer corridor for the bears. Part of this will probably mean trying to get a UBCM resolution passed at its next convention in 2027..
My more immediate actions if I am re-elected would be to increase the fines and enforcement, look into a better system and/or better bear "proof" garbage cans, and restart the free fruit picking for anyone who is unable to do this.

answers.name: Jim Hanson
answers.answer:
Thank you for your advocacy.
Here is my answer:
“Comprehensive bylaws regarding fruit trees in back yards to manage attractants (fruit).”

answers.name: Aidan Kyle
answers.answer:
Thank you for reaching out, and I'm sorry this is a day past your deadline. I agree a bear seen in the neighbourhood shouldn't become a dead bear, and this season has been a hard one.
I believe strongly in a real coexistence model for our community. We live surrounded by forests and creeks, and we do better when we work with nature instead of against it. Bears are the most visible part of that, but coyotes, raccoons and skunks are drawn by the same things, so our approach should cover all of them.
The District already has Bear Smart status, locking carts and fines for leaving garbage out early. So my focus would be on how those rules are actually working. On Council I would push to ask staff for the numbers: how many warnings and fines are issued, where conflicts are happening and what gaps remain, such as apartment and business garbage or fruit trees. I imagine this will also involve taking a look at how district bins play a role in this and whether there’s realistic steps we can take to improve that.
The best tools Council has right now are education and enforcement. It’s clear that current efforts, while present, have been falling short of our goals. I think we have a solid foundation, and we can find a way to improve outcomes for our wildlife.
If you have any more thoughts on this, please don’t hesitate to reach out or to encourage others to. I think it’s important to have the opinion of the community as well as those of experts so that we end up with the best option that protects nature and also reflects our values.

answers.name: Kulvir Mann
answers.answer:
Thank you for your email and question: Besides education, what specific mechanisms would you implement in your municipality to better co-exist with bears?
I have been collaborating with North Shore Black Bear Society to share out education materials to students at schools and parents in the community through my work with North Shore Safety Council for over 10 years.
To move beyond education and create urban co-existance with bears, municilipalities need to enforce the following:
infrastructure upgrades, targeted regulatory penalties and planning solutions.
* Automated Lock-and-Latch Carts - these are the carts everyone has - but residents need to be diligent that there is no damage and they are latched correctly
* Enclosed Commercial Enclosures - small businesses, multi family complexes and parks to house the dumpsters in mandatory heavy duty concrete and steel bear resistant enclosures
* Stricter Curbside Timing and Enforced by Bylaws - for those not following rules to timing of putting out garbage
* Ban High- Attractant Vegetation - update municipal landscaping guidelines to prohibit planting high risk attractants
* Create wildlife corridors - conduct a bear hazard assessment and apply zoning laws to steer bears around residential hubs instead of through them
* Community Fruit Gleaning Network - we already have a lot of volunteers doing this - increase the call out for this and get more people engaged and take part
Education is always important so I would recommend the "Bear Smart Community Program" resources and the key components they have compiled:
Key Components
1. Establish a Bear Smart Committee
Oversees planning and implementation.
Includes local government, wildlife agencies, NGOs, and community members.
2. Conduct a Community Assessment
Identifies attractants (garbage, fruit trees, livestock feed).
Reviews local bear activity and conflict history
3. Develop a Bear Smart Community Plan
Outlines strategies for waste management, education, enforcement, and habitat considerations.
4. Implement the Plan
Install bear‑resistant bins.
Improve bylaws and enforcement.
Conduct public education campaigns.
A brochure outlining the program and a technical background report are available:
Be 'Bear Smart' Community Brochure (PDF, 7MB)
Bear Smart Community Program: Background Report (PDF, 527KB)
I think this is a big issue and we all have to do our part to work collaboratively together and protect the bears and prevent and safety issues that could occur.

answers.name: Linda Munro
answers.answer:
You are the third person to bring up bears to me in the last two days.
I agree, it does seem like we have seen more bear activity this year. Anecdotally, I've heard this; I have also personally had more bear sightings myself this summer than most years. I also saw on Facebook the other day that a bear was spotted at 14th and Lonsdale, a very urban area you would not normally expect to encounter bear activity. This isn't just a North Van phenomenon either, Scott and I were in Osoyoos for a week in August and we saw 4 bears during our time there, and we've never had that happen before in the 12 years since we started taking holidays there.
Whenever I hear about a bear being put down because it has become too habituated to humans I find it very sad.
I am not an expert in bears and so I don't have all the answers. I think you are on the right track of exploring whether there is more we can do. Public education is the right starting point. I would argue we don't do enough in this regard. I think I saw more information about bears circulating 5 or 10 years ago than I do now. So I think we should begin by ramping up education. One new idea, perhaps homeowners could have to complete an online learning module about bear aware living in North Vancouver at the time they pay municipal taxes.
Additionally, it would be good to get some research to inform our next steps to find out:
* what are the primary causes of issues (negligence with garbage, fruit trees in yards, access to fridge or freezer in a garage, deliberately leaving out bear attractants to feed them, etc) ?
* Which areas of the DNV are seeing the highest bear activity, if there is a sub-area that stands out? (so action and education can be concentrated there)
* What can we learn from other forest interface communities about co-existing with bears?
Many thanks,

answers.name: Lisa Muri
answers.answer:
There are multiple factors contributing to bears and conflict, development and clear cutting of habitat, climate change, food sources, reduced ability to monitor garbage (volunteers). Increased bear activity has risen, our fines have done a great deal to reduce bear conflict, but we still need to educate more from a neighbourhood perspective to make sure people understand how to manage attractants. We have carports, fridges and freezers in them, stinky garbage is not being composted, etc. education is the best defence, we have done it before, we need to get volunteers staff council etc to go out and communicate the message. Its not one thing, its multiple approaches.

Reviewing our bylaw in regards to organic waste, enclosed systems to prevent bear access for those who have carports, increased fines, reeducation with direct info on fines and how to manage organic waste.

answers.name: Victoria Nwabuisi
answers.answer:
Thank you for your email.
It is heartbreaking to witness bears being killed in our community. We have moved into their habitat and, as the species with greater power and control, we often expect them to move out. Unfortunately, that is not how coexistence works.
I don’t think dividing ourselves into two camps—the “kill the bears” camp and the “don’t leave attractants out” camp—gets us closer to a solution. It encourages finger-pointing and judgement rather than collaboration.
Ultimately, I believe we can agree on something fundamental: we want people to feel safe, and we want to find a way to live alongside the wildlife that makes North Vancouver such a special place. That is where I would start.
Two concrete steps I would propose are:
1. Strengthen waste management during peak bear season.
Explore prohibiting curbside garbage collection during peak bear season and require residents and commercial properties to use secure, bear-resistant communal waste infrastructure or heavy-duty locking bear bins.
2. Create a community wildlife forum.
Bring together wildlife experts, conservation organizations, residents and community stakeholders for a public forum focused on practical coexistence. The goal would be to better understand what is happening, hear community concerns, examine what is and isn’t working, and identify solutions we can realistically implement.
We cannot undo the fact that we share this landscape with bears. But we can make better choices about how we live alongside them.
Thank you again for the opportunity to share my thoughts.

answers.name: Catherine Pope
answers.answer:
Hi Lindsey and thank you for all the work you do to protect bears on the North Shore. Here is my response to your question and thank you for the opportunity.
Besides education, I would focus on preventing bears from being rewarded with human food.
That means enforcing existing attractant bylaws, particularly around garbage and organics, which are the biggest sources of reported bear attractants on the North Shore. I would also work with bear advocates to identify problem areas and focus municipal resources where they are most needed.
We should also make it easier for residents to do the right thing, including ensuring municipal facilities and public spaces have appropriate systems for securing garbage and other attractants.
Bears don't recognize municipal boundaries, so continued coordination between the three North Shore municipalities, the Bear Society and the Conservation Officer Service is essential. The goal is simple: prevent conflicts before they happen and keep both bears and residents safe.

answers.name: Stephanie Wilson
answers.answer:
My two priorities are:
1. I support tree fruit recovery programs like the North Shore Fruit Tree Project. People may not pick their trees on time for many different reasons so having that service available when folks can't get to their trees is vital. I would love to collaborate to see how the District can better support their work.
2. Better garbage storage for homes without garages/secure storage, i.e. bear-proof trash bin enclosures. Garbage storage can also be an issue for tenants in secondary units when they don't have access to a garage or shed and that also needs to be addressed by the homeowner.
I recognize that fewer bears would be forced into town if they had sufficient food in nature. Work we do to protect wild spaces and use wild spaces responsibly also has an impact on wildlife.
